excerpt: This guide explains how to value and prove non-economic damages for a personal injury settlement.
keyTakeaways: Georgia law allows personal injury victims to recover pain and suffering damages for physical discomfort, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, and disfigurement. Insurers typically calculate these non-economic damages using the multiplier method or per diem method. Georgia does not cap pain and suffering in most cases, but the modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) bars recovery if the victim is 50% or more at fault. The two-year statute of limitations under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 applies to all claims.

faqs.question: Does Georgia cap pain and suffering damages?
faqs.answer: Georgia does not impose a statutory cap on pain and suffering damages in most personal injury cases. However, punitive damages are generally capped at $250,000 under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-5.1 unless the defendant acted with specific intent to harm or was under the influence of drugs or alcohol.

faqs.question: What is the multiplier method for calculating pain and suffering in Georgia?
faqs.answer: The multiplier method takes your total economic damages — medical bills, lost wages, and other out-of-pocket costs — and multiplies them by a factor between 1.5 and 5 depending on the severity and duration of your injuries. More serious injuries with longer recovery periods receive higher multipliers.

faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my pain and suffering award in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Under Georgia's modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), your pain and suffering award is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are found 50% or more at fault for the accident, you are barred from recovering any compensation.

faqs.question: What evidence do I need to prove pain and suffering in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Key evidence includes medical records documenting your injuries and treatment, a personal pain journal recording daily symptoms, testimony from medical experts and mental health professionals, before-and-after statements from family members, and photographs or video showing how your injuries affect your daily life.

faqs.question: How long do I have to file a pain and suffering claim in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations gives you two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. Missing this deadline typically means losing your right to recover compensation, including pain and suffering damages.

faqs.question: Can I recover pain and suffering damages if I had a pre-existing condition?
faqs.answer: Yes. Under Georgia's eggshell plaintiff doctrine, the defendant must compensate you for the full extent of your injuries even if a pre-existing condition made your injuries worse than they would have been for a healthy person. However, you must prove the accident aggravated the pre-existing condition beyond its prior state.
